title: Translation, rotation, scaling, and mirroring
syllabus: Transformation of shapes: translation, rotation, scaling, mirroring
summary: About the origin, a quarter turn and a reflection are coordinate rules. Apply the rule to the vertices; do not redraw the shape from memory.
intuition:
Spatial questions become ordinary arithmetic once each vertex has coordinates. A translation adds the same vector to every point, so lengths and directions are unchanged. A rotation about the origin by a quarter turn is a swap of the coordinates with one sign change. Clockwise sends (x, y) to (y, −x). Counterclockwise sends (x, y) to (−y, x). A half turn sends (x, y) to (−x, −y), which is one quarter turn done twice.

A mirror is also a sign change. Reflection in the x-axis sends (x, y) to (x, −y). Reflection in the y-axis sends (x, y) to (−x, y). Scaling about the origin multiplies both coordinates, or each by its own factor if the stretch is not uniform. Order matters: translate-then-rotate is not rotate-then-translate.

The worked figures below are small on purpose. If you can move three vertices correctly, you can move a letter or an arrow. The picture, when there is one, is only a check on the coordinates already written in the question.

definitions.body: The map $(x,y)\mapsto(x+a,\ y+b)$. Every point moves by the same vector. Shape and size are unchanged.
A turn that fixes (0, 0). The quarter-turn rules are $(x,y)\mapsto(y,-x)$ clockwise and $(x,y)\mapsto(-y,x)$ counterclockwise.
A mirror. In the x-axis, $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$. In the y-axis, $(x,y)\mapsto(-x,y)$.
The map $(x,y)\mapsto(sx,\ ty)$. Uniform scaling has $s=t$ and preserves angles.

formulas.name: Quarter turns
formulas.note: Both are about the origin. A half turn is $(x,y)\mapsto(-x,-y)$.

formulas.name: Mirrors and shift
formulas.note: Reflection in the x-axis, reflection in the y-axis, then a translation.

properties: A translation does not change the vector between two points. A rotation about the origin does not change the distance from the origin.
Two clockwise quarter turns are a half turn. Four clockwise quarter turns are the identity.
Reflecting in the x-axis and then in the y-axis is the half turn $(x,y)\mapsto(-x,-y)$. The order of those two mirrors does not matter.
A clockwise quarter turn and a counterclockwise quarter turn are inverses.
Scaling by a negative factor includes a half turn. Scaling by −1 is exactly the half turn.

examples.title: One point, four maps
examples.prompt: Apply a clockwise quarter turn, a counterclockwise quarter turn, a half turn, and a reflection in the x-axis to the point (3, 1). All turns are about the origin.
steps: Clockwise quarter turn: (x, y) goes to (y, −x), so (3, 1) goes to (1, −3).
Counterclockwise quarter turn: (x, y) goes to (−y, x), so (3, 1) goes to (−1, 3).
Half turn: (3, 1) goes to (−3, −1). Reflection in the x-axis keeps x and flips y, so (3, 1) goes to (3, −1).

examples.title: A triangle rotated a quarter turn clockwise
examples.prompt: The triangle has vertices (0, 0), (2, 0), and (2, 1). Rotate it 90 degrees clockwise about the origin and list the images.
steps: (2, 0) goes to (0, −2) by the rule (x, y) → (y, −x).
(2, 1) goes to (1, −2). The right angle that was at (2, 0) is now at (0, −2), still a right angle, and the size is unchanged.

traps: Using (y, x) for a quarter turn and forgetting the sign. (3, 1) clockwise is (1, −3), not (1, 3).
Rotating about a corner as if it were the origin. The rules on this page fix (0, 0). A different centre needs a translation to the origin, the turn, and a translation back.
Reflecting in the wrong axis. The x-axis flips the second coordinate. The y-axis flips the first.
Adding the translation before the rotation and expecting the same result as the other order. (x+a, y+b) rotated is not (x, y) rotated and then shifted by (a, b).

questions.stem: The point (4, 2) is rotated 90 degrees clockwise about the origin. Its image is
questions.solution: The answer is **A**. The clockwise rule is (x, y) → (y, −x), so (4, 2) → (2, −4). Option B is the counterclockwise image. Option C is the half turn. Option D is the reflection in the x-axis.

questions.stem: The point (4, 2) is reflected in the y-axis and the image is then translated by (1, −3). The final point is
questions.solution: The answer is **A**. Reflection in the y-axis sends (4, 2) to (−4, 2). Adding (1, −3) gives (−3, −1). Option B translates before reflecting. Option C adds the translation in the wrong direction on x.

questions.stem: Which of the following maps send (3, 1) to (−3, −1)?
options: A half turn about the origin.
Reflection in the x-axis followed by reflection in the y-axis.
One clockwise quarter turn about the origin.
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and D**. A half turn sends (x, y) to (−x, −y). Reflecting in both axes does the same, and scaling by −1 is that map. One clockwise quarter turn sends (3, 1) to (1, −3).

questions.stem: A triangle has vertices (0, 0), (2, 0), and (2, 1). After a 90 degree clockwise rotation about the origin, which of the following are vertices of the image?
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and C**. The images are (0, 0), (0, −2), and (1, −2). The point (−2, 0) would be the image of (0, 2), which is not a vertex of this triangle.

questions.stem: The point (5, −2) is rotated 180 degrees about the origin. Enter the x-coordinate of the image.
questions.solution: The answer is **−5**. A half turn sends (x, y) to (−x, −y), so the image is (−5, 2) and the x-coordinate is −5.
